KATAZA - baboon relocation

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The baboon that has made headlines around the world and caused a social media storm is being moved to a rehabilitation centre in limpopo.

Unique Selling Point:
We have an exclusive which i have brokered with Jaco Pieterse from SPCA. It wont be known anywhere else, and they wont post video's. They are going to try capture him in a cage first, which will likely be unsuccessful but they need to try first. then tomorrow they will dart him. There is quite a team they have got together to handle the movement of the baboon after that and he's going to a rehab in limpopo.

Summary:
Plan: We would film the darting or capture of kataza in a cage, get interviews with inspectors on the scene and SPCA.
Get an interview with Cape Nature and comment from city of Cape Town who made the decision on them taking him away in the first place from the slangkop troop.
The Limpopo rehab is riverside wildlife rehab centre 015 345 1050. We will speak to them about what to expect, integration etc


Further information:
We will chat to ICWILD who know a lot about human and animal conflict - esp when it comes to baboons. They have the science and usually these animals are put down. They are in partnership with university of cape town. http://www.icwild.uct.ac.za/contact-27
General enquiries
Email: icwild@uct.ac.za
Institute directors
Justin O'Riain (justin.oriain@uct.ac.za), University of Cape Town
Nicoli Nattrass (nicoli.nattrass@uct.ac.za), University of Cape Town

INterview Jaco Pieterse and his team of vets and inspectors who will move the baboon.
Then we will ask cape nature for an interview as well.
Cape Nature
For communications and media enquiries, please contact Petro van Rhyn – General Manager: Advocacy
Tel: 087 087 9262
Cell number: 071 2317576
Email: pvrhyn@capenature.co.za


Extra Budget Items:
Flight to cape town sasha -
the rehab centre is in tzaneen - so i'll ask them to take video there and send it to me of the release.

I think we have greg going now - if there is drama... I dont think we'll be able to have a presenter :( so we save costs there...

Script:


Meet Kataza - this was his last day living as a free Cape Chacma baboon...
TWO WEEKS AGO KATAZA’S FUTURE HUNG IN A PRECARIOUS BALANCE – THERE WERE ARGUMENTS BY SCIENTISTS, GOVERNMENT AND HOME OWNERS TO EUTHANIZE HIM, WHILE OTHERS LIKE THE SPCA AND ANIMAL RIGHTS ACTIVISTS THOUGHT HE COULD BE REHABILITATED. BUT HOW DID IT COME TO THIS, AND WHY HAS THIS SPLIT THE CAPE TOWN COMMUNITY? FADE TO BLACK
Kataza lived with his troop near Kommetjie - a town on the Cape peninsula.
Jenni: Apart from his one missing canine, and he's a very laid back and gentle baboon.
Animal activist Jenni Trethowan manages the baboon matters trust. She first noticed Kataza was missing.
Jenni: It was only four days later that the authorities admitted that they had moved Kataza.
That authority was the City of Cape Town who deemed him a problem animal that habitually raided urban areas. Subsequently they’d moved him 20km away to Tokai instead of opting for euthenasia. The city's mayoral committee member Alderman Marian Nieuwhoudt says all other preventative methods had been exhausted.
Marian: if the animals have learned their behavior, the more difficult it is to take the the lead animal out of it.
Animal welfare organizations were not a part of this decision, says Chief Inspector at the Cape of Good Hope SPCA Jaco Pieterse.
Jaco: We believe had the various role players been consulted, this whole debacle could have been avoided. We wanted all avenues to first be explored for the city to be transparent.
Jenni: So I believe that the city of Cape Town relied on data gathered and what we have contested is that that data wasn't completely accurate.
But behavioural ecologist Esme Beamish who studies baboons at the University of Cape Town argues the decision was scientifically sound.
Esme: Obviously when you've got five million people surrounding approximately 500 baboons, you have potential for conflict. So you will help a male move from a troop where he would be breeding with his own family, to a troop where he breeds with unrelated females. We've relocated 16 baboons in the peninsula and 60 percent of them integrate.
Director of the institute for communities and wildlife in Africa Justin O’Riain has published extensively on peninsula baboons.
Justin: There are people in that community who believe baboons should share space with people. And so that makes it an extraordinarily difficult place to manage baboons.
THOUGHTS: 1. KATAZA MEANS ‘NUISANCE” AND LIKE HIS NAME – THE BABOON RAIDED HOMES AND BUSINESSES. 2. HE IS DOING WHAT COMES NATURALLY TO HIM – FINDING FOOD – AND HUMANS WHO LIVE IN THE AREA SHOULD BE AWARE THAT THEY NEED TO BABOON PROOF THEIR HOMES.
Jaco: The baboons have been around for hundreds of years and we as people have moved into their living space. So we as people need to amend our lifestyles so that we don't attract the baboons into our homes because we are being negligent.
In 2000, a primatologist created the city’s baboon management protocols which they say have successfully reduced baboon deaths by human intervention by keeping them out of urban areas 80% of the time.
So the best thing for baboons and their conservation and their well-being is to keep them out of urban spaces. And hence, the baboon management program has evolved. He had been severely habituated by people during lockdown. So the authorities felt that he they were mitigating circumstances. And the only other option in terms of the guidelines was relocation.
Cape Nature which regulates environmental legislation issued a permit for his relocation, says its nature operations executive director Ernst Baard.
Ernst: So in in the in the case of SK11, We have adopted several best practice guidelines we are very strong following the science based approach to our conservation.
Jenni: So we did a review of all the management data you can see that removing individual animals does not solve the problem.
Trethowan began the social media campaign called “Bring Kataza Back,” and while visiting him in Tokai, Kataza recognized her.
Jenni: I thought maybe he would walk with me and then he wouldn't feel quite so vulnerable. So I started walking with them and he started walking with me.
Over the next two months Kataza began interacting with a local troop.
Esme: So he showed all the signs of integration is the main problem was that he still wanted to go on urban areas.
But then a court order was granted to return Kataza. The application was brought by insolvency practitioner and concerned citizen Ryno Englebrecht.
Englebrecht: A few of my wealthy friends and colleagues phoned me and advised me that he’s not settling in, And I brought a court application against the city of Cape Town, to review the decision. The application was settled and Kataza was relocated back to his native troop.
Many believe people interfered in Kataza’s integration process which was also too short.
video of humans feeding kataza
Esme: The lobby groups thought that he was missing his family and he would go back to Kommetjie and be accepted and be delighted to see everyone? He spent two days and the proximity of them. And the reason was simply this, that he'd become aware of unrelated females. And that's what he wants in his life.
But many social media wannabe primatologists fought online about Kataza’s saga.
Jenni: The incredible social media attention took me by surprise. kataza just was the most incredible, perfect storm.
Justin: We lost the communications battle because it takes two or three years to produce a scientific paper that would have explained the value of dispersing and outbreeding.
LINK: THE THING ABOUT BABOONS IS THAT THEY ARE SO HUMAN LIKE THAT MANY PEOPLE BECOME EMOTIONAL ABOUT THE CREATURE, BUT MANY CONSERVATIONISTS STRESS THAT SOMETIMES WHEN IT COMES TO WHAT IS BEST FOR A TROOP OR THE ENVIRONMENT OR HUMANS LIVING IN AN AREA, CULLING AN ANIMAL IS THE MOST ETHICAL AND COST EFFECTIVE MEASURE.
After Kataza failed to reintegrate with his troop, the SPCA stepped in.
Jaco: The SPCA proposed that Kataza be translocated to the Riverside Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre in Limpopo. We believe it is the only option for him to have a good life in a semi wild environment. So at least he won't be stuck in a cage forever. He will be in a 600 hectare enclosure with other baboons.
That rehab is run by primatologist Bob Venter whose worked with baboons for 30 years.
Bob: Kataza is a legend, deserves a normal life.
CAPTURE SEQUENCE
Jaco: We safely darted kataza with the assistance of two veterinarians and various tests that have been done, which was part of the permit conditions.
He then began his almost 2000km trip to his new home.
LINK: KATAZAS LIFE AT THE REHAB BEGAN THIS WEEK …
Bob: And I cried like a young kid, just being grateful that we can save this animal.
Jaco: They've got many years of experience with rehabilitating primates.
But how do we avoid more Kataza’s in Cape Town's future? Scientists have proposed contraception, baboon proof fences – others euthanasia, while activists want the bylaws and protocls to change.
Engelbrecht has taken further court action against the city.
Engelbrecht: And they must utilize the services of not only public participation, but also qualified primatologist, and I'm further asking to that order, that Cape nature be ordered to oversee the enforcement of the permit.
Marian: We've really bent over backwards to do whatever we can to the benefit of both humans and baboons.
Jaco: We cannot have a situation like this reoccurring in the future. The baboon protocols must be reviewed and they must be amended so that it benefits the well-being of both the people and the animals that are affected at the end of the day. 8:08
